E0526.summary: Paracelsus's term, used by Atwood in the Appendix for the dream of its whole afterlife the soul brings into the body, its destiny; God's grace is the Divine evestrum relative to man.
E0526.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood takes up Paracelsus's term: “the soul comes into this body with the dream of its whole afterlife presented to it” [APP ¶57]. This is its destiny, which moves a will that does not see beyond it. Against it stands “God’s grace (the Divine evestrum, relatively to man)” [APP ¶57], by which, Atwood says, we overcome it.

E0527.summary: What the abusers of the art succeeded in inducing before denying the Light its fulfilment; not further defined.
E0527.body: Atwood (her own voice) says the abusers of the work denied the Light its fulfilment after “having succeeded in inducing an exalted energy” [III.4 ¶6]. The text does not define the expression further.

forms: the excellent author of the Aquarium Sapientum, or Water Stone
the pious author of the Aquarium
E0528.summary: The author of the Aquarium Sapientum, or Water Stone, cited by Atwood for the spirit-soul-body cycle and for the warning that pride or covetousness makes the art vanish.
E0528.body: Atwood cites this author from the Aquarium Sapientum (in the Musaeum Hermeticum) for a Latin enigma illustrating the separation, putrefaction and reunion of spirit, soul and body: “Spiritus ipse datur pro tempore corpori” [I.3 n21] (our rendering: the spirit itself is given to the body for a time). Elsewhere, as “the pious author of the Aquarium”, he supports her point that pride or covetousness after possession makes the art disappear: “this art will vanish from under thy hands” [III.4 ¶7; III.4 n4]. Atwood endorses this warning.

E0529.summary: In the verse Hunting of the Greene Lyon, the residue taken away once the matter has grown very dry, before the young Child is lodged in a bright bed.
E0529.body: The word occurs in the quoted verse of The Hunting of the Greene Lyon: when the matter has grown very dry, “The excrements be tane away;” [III.1 ¶65], before the young Child is laid in a bright bed. The voice is the quoted poem, not Atwood's own.

E0530.summary: The law of Universal nature, whose fountain Atwood names as the Substant Unity.
E0530.body: Atwood speaks of the Substant Unity as “the fountain of Universal nature and her Exemplary Law” [III.3 ¶79]. The text gives no further definition.

E0531.summary: That without which, Atwood says, every plan of improvement is defective; not further defined.
E0531.body: Atwood judges “every plan defective without the Exemplary Light” [IV.4 ¶18]. The expression is not further defined in the records.

E0532.summary: In Atwood's words, the Logos hidden and slain from the foundation in the fiat of our Identity, occulted in two diametrically reverse poles or principles.
E0532.body: Atwood writes that “the exemplary Logos is hidden, --- slain from the foundation in the exterminating fiat of our Identity” [III.3 ¶79]; its occultation lies in two diametrically reverse poles or principles. The text does not define it further.

E0533.summary: Atwood's qualifier for Part I's outer view of the progress and theory of alchemy, used in the heading.
E0533.body: The word appears in the heading of Part I: “An Exoteric View of the Progress and Theory of Alchemy” [I.1 ¶1]. Its sense is not further explained in the records; the heading apparently marks Part I as the outward, historical treatment.

E0534.summary: In the verse Tablet, a personified creative power that framed all things from nothing; in Atwood's prose, the resulting experience of life, third of the alchemical Three.
E0534.body: The voice is unclear. In the verse rendering of the Tablet the speaker addresses Experience as a creative power: “That thou art the very same, That didst from nothing all things frame;” [III.3 ¶76], having made the One Thing. In the following prose Atwood speaks of the Matter proved simple in experience and of “the resulting experience of life” [III.3 ¶77] as the third of the alchemical Three. How the personified power and the third principle relate is not stated; the records leave both readings side by side.

E0535.summary: An unnamed authority Atwood relies on for man's connection to the fountain of Universal Nature.
E0535.body: Atwood appeals to “the experienced” without naming them, on the point of our connection to the fountain of the Universal Nature [II.4 ¶19].

E0536.summary: Atwood's word for the practical hermetic work itself, seldom attempted and more rarely completed, through which the ancients found their whole philosophy and the Fathers came into Experience.
E0536.body:
In Atwood's own voice the Experiment is the practical work: “That was the Experiment that led our Fathers into Experience” [III.3 ¶61], and experience is the proper test of philosophy. She insists on perseverance for it (“than perseverance for this experiment” [III.4 ¶45]). She explains “why the Divine Experiment has been so seldom attempted and more rarely brought to a legitimate conclusion on this earth” [IV.4 ¶7], and says “In the course of this vital experiment the ancients discovered the whole of the philosophy they teach” [IV.4 ¶9]. She identifies it with a “pyrotechnical induction” of “the quintessence of Universal nature and her fruitful springs” [IV.4 ¶9].

The adjective “experimental” carries the same weight in Part I: Democritus is styled “the father of experimental philosophy” and “Pliny bears witness to the experimental fame of Democritus, and his skill in the occult sciences and practice of them” [I.1 ¶12]; Aristotle “led mankind astray from the path of true experiment” [I.1 ¶16]; the theosophic schools are “based on a similar experimental ground” [I.1 ¶17], where practical science is set against abstracts. Contrast Atwood's critical use of “experimental philosophy” for modern science [IV.4 ¶30].

E0537.summary: The voice cited from the Philosophical Epitaph of W.C., cited for the reversal of death in the work.
E0537.body: Atwood cites the title page of the Philosophical Epitaph of W.C. to illustrate the overcoming of death in the work: “O death how art thou vanquished” [I.3 n43].

E0538.summary: What the soul has not yet attained while she regards her image objectively and is 'in Hades'.
E0538.body: Atwood describes the soul, while she regards her image objectively and is in Hades, as being “before attaining to the experimental knowledge” [II.3 ¶36]. The term is not further defined here; the context suggests a knowing by inward experience as opposed to outward regard.

E0539.summary: Atwood's name for modern science following Lord Bacon's 'exterminating chase', which she says labours for selfish aggrandizement.
E0539.body: Atwood, in her own voice, criticizes modern science led by Lord Bacon's “exterminating chase”: “experimental philosophy labours for selfish aggrandizement” [IV.4 ¶30].

E0540.summary: The practical stage of the art, which follows study of the doctrine.
E0540.body: Atwood distinguishes study of the doctrine from what “is afterwards needed for the experimental proof” [III.4 ¶15], that is, the practical stage of the art.

E0541.summary: A required means of approaching the secrets of the highest causes, which Atwood compares to Charon's fee.
E0541.body: Atwood states: “neither are the secrets of the highest causes approached without a mean of expiation” [III.2 ¶44], comparing it to the fee paid to Charon. What the expiation consists of is not spelled out in the record.

E0542.summary: Unnamed interpreters of the Mysteries whose narcotic explanation of initiatory transfiguration Atwood rejects.
E0542.body: Atwood reports the expounders' view that “all this splendid delirium and transfiguration in the Mysteries was the effect of narcotic liquors” [II.4 ¶56], and rejects it as common sense acting Procrustes-like.

E0543.summary: In the Appendix, the means by which the desire of the lower life opens into the heart life.
E0543.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood describes the desire of the lower life “opening up into the heart life, or the medial life, or the celestial life, or the vegetable life, by exstasis” [APP ¶97]. The four names given there are apparently treated as equivalent.

E0544.summary: Outer and inner reality, which at the completion of the work are seen to blend and confirm each other.
E0544.body: Atwood writes that at the completion “the External and Internal Worlds were seen to blend together in confluent harmony” [III.3 ¶82], each confirming the other.

E0545.summary: In Eirenaeus, the well-regulated outward heat that alone assists Nature in the Second operation.
E0545.body: Quoting Eirenaeus, Atwood gives the Second operation as performed by Nature “by the sole assistance of a well-regulated external fire” [IV.1 ¶11].

E0546.summary: Boehme's term for the outward self, which could hardly grasp or express what he had seen inwardly.
E0546.body: In a passage Atwood quotes from Boehme, he says of his inward vision: “I could very hardly apprehend the same in my external man” [III.2 ¶16].

E0547.summary: A Hermetic writer Atwood lists among Paracelsus's worthy disciples and in the 'golden chain' of Hermetic philosophers who traced the poets' allusions.
E0547.body: Faber is listed in a note with the work Opera Medico-Chimica [I.1 ¶70; I.1 n88]. Atwood names him with Van Helmont, Crollius, Fludd and Helvetius as intelligent, worthy disciples of Paracelsus [I.1 ¶64], and with Plato, Proclus, Porphyry, Tollius and Michael Maier in the “golden chain of Hermetic philosophers” who traced the poets' allusions and claimed Homer and Virgil as their own; she cites them in support [III.1 ¶25]. In an aside on Ripley's method the text remarks: “Faber is so wise that he will not understand him” [IV.1 ¶36].

E0548.summary: The fable of Isis feeding Horus with fire, cited to illustrate nourishing the son with fire.
E0548.body: Atwood cites the fable in which “she brought forth Horus, even feeding him with fire” [I.3 n41], to illustrate the nourishing of the son with fire.

forms: fable of Mars and Venus taken together by Vulcan
E0549.summary: The fable cited to illustrate the need of the masculine tincture with Venus, with fuller explanation deferred.
E0549.body: Atwood cites the fable of Mars and Venus caught together by Vulcan to illustrate the need of the masculine tincture with Venus, promising to explain it later [I.3 n49].

forms: the fable (Typhon, Osiris, Isis; the Egyptian monarch)
E0550.summary: The Egyptian fable of Typhon, Osiris and Isis, read by Atwood as a figure of the threefold division of the ethereal hypostasis and the reconciling of opposites.
E0550.body: Atwood reads the fable that “Typhon killed Osiris, his uterine brother, and scattered his members to the four winds” [III.1 ¶53] as illustrating the threefold division of the ethereal hypostasis; the hair grown in Ethiopia figures the fire allowed to grow [III.1 ¶56]; and Isis figures the reconciling of the opposites [III.1 ¶63].

forms: the fables (Theseus, Ariadne, Jason, Medea, Hercules, Eurystheus, Achilles, Ulysses, Minerva, Aeneas, the Sybil)
E0551.summary: The heroic fables Atwood cites to show that the hero never labours alone but is aided by wise counsel, as the Moon aids the seeking Reason.
E0551.body: Atwood draws on the fables of Theseus and Ariadne, Jason and Medea, Hercules and Eurystheus, Achilles, Ulysses and Minerva, Aeneas and the Sybil to show that the hero never labours alone but is aided by wise counsel, as the Moon or Passive Intelligence aids the seeking Reason [III.1 ¶40].

E0552.summary: The intellect which, Atwood says, is not born without Motion, figured by Pallas brought forth from Jove with Vulcan's aid.
E0552.body: Atwood writes: “without the instrumentality of Motion, which the lame god personates, the Fabricate Intellect is not born” [IV.1 ¶34]. The figure is Pallas brought forth from Jove with Vulcan's help; Vulcan, the lame god, stands for Motion (stated).

E0553.summary: In the cabalistic scriptures and antique schools Atwood reports, a higher faculty latent in man which, revealed, knows nature intuitively and works magically as her source.
E0553.body: Reporting the cabalistic scriptures and schools of antique experience, Atwood speaks of “the germ of a higher faculty or Wisdom” [II.1 ¶32] in man, which, revealed and set alone, knows nature intuitively and works magically as her substratal source. It is identified with “This Being” (“This Being, moreover, or Faculty of Wisdom” [II.1 ¶32]).

E0554.summary: The earthy residue of the matter: in Hermes the third from two, from which death is removed; in Sendivogius cast away; in Eudoxus kept and washed, as hiding the Balm of Life.
E0554.body: The records come from three quoted authorities, who differ on its handling. In a Hermetic passage it is the third of the three that come from two, the earth that remains below, and death is to be taken away: “death from the faeces” [I.3 ¶23]. Sendivogius has the residue discarded after putrefaction, before the spirit is returned to the water: “the faeces being cast away” [III.3 ¶29]. Eudoxus, by contrast, says the black earthy residue at the bottom of the vessel must not be discarded: “The Balm of Life is hid in these unclean faeces” [IV.3 ¶8]; it is washed with the celestial water until it is no longer black. Whether these describe different stages or different practices is not settled by the records.

E0555.summary: Cited for the soul's permanent union with the glorified body, as an analogy for the union of spirits and purified bodies in the work.
E0555.body: The doctrine of Faith is invoked as an analogy: as the soul is permanently united with the glorified body, so spirits and purified bodies are joined, and “there shall be no more separation or death” [IV.3 ¶10].
